documents.unit: Office of Community Standards / Board on Conduct Affairs
documents.title: Generative AI Policy Guidance
documents.summary: Stanford's Board on Conduct Affairs, adopted in February 2023, says that unless an instructor states otherwise, generative AI use is treated like help from another person and may not be used to substantially complete assignments or exams. Instructors may set their own rules, should put them in the syllabus, and may warn students about detection software. Students should acknowledge AI use and ask when unsure.
documents.stance_why: The document gives a fallback ("treated analogously to assistance from another person") but says "Individual course instructors are free to set their own policies ... allowing or disallowing some or all uses", so the decision is handed to instructors and the document is coded delegates, not restrict.

units.why: The BCA states its purpose: "To give sufficient space for instructors to explore uses of generative AI tools" and "set clear guidelines to students". This is a statement of scope and purpose for the institution-level guidance, so it is general and informational, and P56 (framework and purpose) fits better than P04 because it explains why the guidance exists rather than assigning the decision.
units.anchor: To give sufficient space for instructors to explore uses of generative AI tools
units.frag_start: To give sufficient space for instructors
units.frag_end: consistent with the Stanford Honor Code

units.why: The page says generative AI tools "have applications that foster student learning and understanding", which names a benefit of AI for learning without making it a rule, so P87 (benefits) fits rather than P44 (career skill).
units.anchor: these tools have applications that foster student learning and understanding

units.why: The page warns that the tools "can also be used in ways that bypass key learning objectives", a reason for limiting some uses because they undercut learning. P41 is the nearest type, but the passage does not say practice builds skill, only that learning objectives are bypassed.
units.anchor: these tools can also be used in ways that bypass key learning objectives
units.frag_start: these tools can also be used
units.fit_note: Says AI can bypass learning objectives; does not say that doing the work yourself builds skill.

units.why: "Absent a clear statement from a course instructor" sets what applies when the instructor is silent, so this is a fallback rule (P06). The same sentence also treats AI like another person (coded separately as P45); I chose P06 here because this anchor is the silence condition.
units.anchor: consultation with generative AI shall be treated analogously to assistance from another person
units.frag_start: Absent a clear statement from a
units.policy: Absent a clear statement from a course instructor, use of or consultation with generative AI is treated analogously to assistance from another person.
units.fit_note: The fallback is not a ban: AI is treated like help from another person, which is allowed or not depending on Honor Code rules for such help.

units.why: The default rule that AI "shall be treated analogously to assistance from another person" equates AI with a human helper under existing Honor Code rules, which is P45. P06 is coded on the same sentence for its silence condition; this unit captures the analogy itself.
units.anchor: treated analogously to assistance from another person
units.frag_start: Absent a clear statement from a

units.why: "using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam ... is not permitted" bans having AI produce the submitted work, including by entering exam or assignment questions, so P19 is the type (P20 and P22 are only partly implied).
units.anchor: using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam
units.frag_start: In particular, using generative AI tools
units.frag_end: by entering exam or assignment questions) is not permitted
units.policy: Using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam (e.g. by entering exam or assignment questions) is not permitted.
units.fit_note: Also names entering exam or assignment questions as an example of the banned use, which overlaps P20 and P22.

units.why: "Students should acknowledge the use of generative AI (other than incidental use)" asks for acknowledgment of AI use in submissions, with incidental use excluded, so P24 fits; the incidental exemption is part of the same sentence, so I did not split it into P100.
units.anchor: Students should acknowledge the use of generative AI (other than incidental use)
units.fit_note: Excludes incidental use from the disclosure expectation.

units.why: "default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt" tells students to lean toward disclosure when unsure whether disclosure is needed. It is a distinct rule from the acknowledgment expectation and best fits P24, since nothing about penalties or safety is stated (P28 does not fit).
units.anchor: default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt
units.frag_end: disclosing such assistance when in doubt

units.why: "Individual course instructors are free to set their own policies" hands the allow-or-disallow decision to each instructor, which is P04 and is the reason the document is coded as delegating.
units.anchor: Individual course instructors are free to set their own policies regulating the use
units.frag_start: Individual course instructors are free to
units.frag_end: some or all uses of such tools

units.why: "Course instructors should set such policies in their course syllabi and clearly communicate such policies to students" asks instructors to put AI rules in the syllabus, which is P09.
units.anchor: Course instructors should set such policies in their course syllabi and clearly communicate
units.frag_start: Course instructors should set such policies

units.why: "Students who are unsure of policies regarding generative AI tools are encouraged to ask their instructors for clarification" tells students to ask when unsure, which is P10.
units.anchor: Students who are unsure of policies regarding generative AI tools are encouraged to ask
units.frag_start: Students who are unsure of policies

units.why: OCS "recommends course instructors provide clear advance notice that they may use detection software to review work submitted for use of generative AI". It is a recommendation about telling students that detection may be used. P40 is the nearest type (detection tools used) but the passage is about advance notice, not the method of use.

units.frag_start: OCS recommends course instructors provide clear
units.frag_end: submitted for use of generative AI
units.fit_note: Passage is about giving students advance notice that detection software may be used, not about how detection is used.

units.why: "The BCA will continue to monitor developments in these tools ... and may update this guidance" states that the guidance is provisional and will be revisited, which is P54.

notes: Only the Generative AI Policy Guidance section of the saved BCA page was coded. The rest (hearing panels, hearing examiners, proctoring, penalty code, withdrawal statement, enrollment holds) is not about AI and was skipped. The proctoring guidance bans remote proctoring but says nothing about AI.
